A year ago, I installed a 5kW system with Growatt inverter. The installation was quick and efficient as was the customer service. The system worked so well, that I installed another 5kW system early this year which was also a response to increases in power prices. This time, a Goodwe was installed as Growatt were no longer available.  This too is working well now. Initially, the Goodwe inverter kept tripping out during the best part of the day when the sun was shining. The front panel showed a Vac error, which meant the line voltage was too high. I measured it at over 262V. Inverters are designed to protect themselves and shut down with a high line voltage is detected. Also, each solar inverter contributes a small rise to the line voltage of about 3V. It turned out my Growatt inverter was raising the line voltage just high enough to trip out the Goodwe. This problem has been fixed by adjusting the trip out voltage setting for the Goodwe. I note that many reviewers have reported problems with their inverters, but it may not be the fault of the inverter at all. High line voltages are common and can be caused by too many solar inverters nearby on the same network, or a failed voltage regulator which has also happened to me. It is the responsibility of the power network company to fix high line voltages, not the solar installer. What the solar installer can do is to ensure that the inverter trip out voltage is set high. Many solar owners are unaware that their systems are not working as they should which is why monitoring performance is so important. You want the best return on your investment. Most inverter manufacturers have a wifi monitoring system built in, and once set up is free to use. Alternatively, you can just check the front panel.

This is probably more detail than you wanted, but I'm a writer, so, hey.True Value Solar was one of six companies that quoted. I specified a 5kW system based on my average power bill of $450 per two months, to be installed on a sundrenched flat, slightly east-tilting Colorbond roof. Tilted panel frames 30 deg to north was an optional extra I wanted quoted separately. The quotes were around $50 per panel (total around $1000 extra). I ultimately declined, fully aware of the drop in efficiency I experience. But Perth has a lot of bright sunlight all through the year, and I mostly wanted the system for free air conditioning in summer. I'm retired and spend a lot of time at home during the day, which is when the system delivers. If I get 3.5 kW I will be happy. If I don't I can always tilt them later.There was a staggeringly wide range of prices, deals, offers and embarrassingly pitiful pleads to get my business. The prices ranged from $5400 to over $22,000 (this is not a typo). Some panels and inverters offered were difficult to find on the internet, which rang alarm bells immediately. Three of the six companies told me they were the largest in the state. I guess superlatives aren't what they used to be.After considerable research (two weeks Google-reading and talking to supplier reps) I decided an acceptable risk-balance of quality, cost, reputability and longevity of manufacturers would be Chinese made Renesolar 250 Watt tier one panels and a German SMA three phase inverter. My Perth home is three phased, but Western Power restricts export from domestic power plants to a maximum of 2.5 kW per phase.True Value Solar is a remote company, and it is doubtful you'll ever meet a rep. I have only ever communicated with them by email and phone, and I suspect no one I spoke to was a permanent employee. I imagine it has huge bulk-buying power; clever financial people; a huge TV ad budget; a roomful of tele-sales people on commission; and a network of low margin electrical contractors at their disposal in all states. They also have an annoying bulk mentality to their customers. For example I received repeated SMS reminders to complete and submit paperwork even though I had done so on the day I received it. After complaining about this they told me it was just standard practice to hurry up stragglers (i.e it was standard practice to annoy their customers).I paid $500 deposit by credit card to True Value Solar on 31 Jan 2014. They had already alerted me installation would be 6 to 8 weeks away, which was fine. True to their word, on week seven Western Power installed the import-export meter, and on Thursday 20 March TVS called to say installation was arranged for the following Monday 25 March. They asked for payment either by credit card there and then, or by bank cheque to be given to the installers. Payment in advance is always risky so I opted for the bank cheque to retain some control.The installers were called Ab Fab Electrical. I imagine it's pot luck which installer you get with TVS. Note: WA-based quotes made a point of emphasising they use in-house electricians. I'm still not sure that's a good thing. Anyway Ab Fab arrived on time, but there was an initial problem because they had brought the wrong panels. This was quickly fixed and the Renesolar panels were miraculously delivered within the hour. A suspicious mind could imagine many reasons why the wrong panels were brought (a brand I'd never heard of) but I will give Ab Fab the benefit of the doubt. And I can well imagine their communications with True Value Solar is as remote as anyones. However if I hadn't checked I'd now be blissfully ignorant of what was on the roof, or arguing with TVS to replace them, which I suspect would take a Court Order. Lesson: Always check what's delivered.Installation was good quality (I have some experience of electrics) and I couldn't fault anything major that Ab Fab did. They were good guys, polite, eager to please and solar-experienced. There was a minor issue with my old circuit breakers, which was quickly sorted satisfactorily; and a cringe-moment when the apprentice accidentally drilled a small hole into a bedroom ceiling cornice thinking it was the wall cavity. They offered to get it repaired at their cost, but it wasn't a big deal. I also know how easy it is to make that mistake because identifying ceiling edges in 100-year-old houses with insulated pressed tin ceilings is almost impossible unless you've got x-ray vision, they built them differently back then. A little Spak-filler made it go away.Summary: All in all, I believe I received a very good deal: 20 panels and a high quality inverter, installed on schedule with minimum hassle for $5979. I must say True Value Solar didn't go out of their way to make me feel good about having chosen them; and there's always a small voice in my head saying what do I do if the system fails and they stop answering
